pr_body:
Fixes #17413.

Fixing this without reregressing #16922 is a bit of a puzzle. This solution should keep both issues fixed while also dynamically determining the strafing run trajectory based on weapon range and turn speed instead of relying on an arbitrary tick count.

The one problem with this solution is that it changes aircraft to immediately cancel the attack when the target is killed instead of moving towards the last known position of the target when it was alive. Now, I do think that this is a good thing in and of itself (and we should do that for the other activities as well), but my current implementation would also leak the status of hidden targets. I haven't found a simple way to distinguish between actors that died while visible and actors that died while hidden under fog, so I hope that someone else has an idea for how to do this. If not, then I think this may be the lesser evil for the short term.

Incidentally, this also adds the correct behaviour for `Aircraft.MoveWithinRange` applied to fixed-wing aircraft and a minimum range.
pr_comments:
> I haven't found a simple way to distinguish between actors that died while visible and actors that died while hidden under fog

I'm not sure whether your PRs have changed this, but when I implemented the system we could distinguish these by looking at both target and lastvisibletarget: actors that died while hidden will have `target` as invalid, `lastVisibleTarget` as valid; actors that died while visible will have both invalid.
Ah right, I was misremembering. The `targetIsHiddenActor` bool provides the additional context, not `lastVisibleTarget`.
OK. I figured it out now.

I think we need to be careful here about pushing too much behaviour down into `MoveWithinRange`. IMO it is completely reasonable to expect that aircraft may want to behave differently when ordered to generically move into range of a target vs being ordered to attack said target (consider long strafing runs).

I think there may be some confusion here. I deliberately _did_ make the behaviour in `MoveWithinRange` generic. In order to get the specific strafing behaviour I used the 'trick' of using a minimum range of zero on the incoming flight and the maximum weapon range as minimum range on the return flight.
Aha, that makes more sense. Can you please put a comment before the `MoveWithinRange` call in `FlyAttack` explaining this?

Updated:
- Take account of frozen actors
- Changed `AttackTurnDelay` to `AttackRunLength` and added update rule.
- Added comment to `FlyAttack`

issue_context.title: Planes don't turn towards their target if it is in weapon range
issue_context.body:
## This release
![RegressedMiG](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/37534529/69955875-5bf5a100-1507-11ea-9021-2e8b07059446.gif) 
## Last release
![NormalMiG](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/37534529/69955869-59934700-1507-11ea-82c3-d7ab8d1c64bc.gif)

When a target in range is selected planes instead of turning towards it try their hardest to complete the strafe. It makes microing aircraft significantly harder as you have to manually turn them towards their target for them to actually shoot. We had dozens of reports on Discord about how unresponsive MiGs are, it is a major regression and needs to be addressed in the hotfix
comments: Modern planes woudn't need to turn (depending on the type of weapon), so I suggest making this optional at the mod level.
Modern planes *probably* have the ability to fire their weapons while facing in a different direction to the target to go with that ;)

*Some modern or futuristic planes in some potential mods may have weapons that they can fire at a target without having to face it directly. So I suggest making this optional at the mod level, **ideally per-weapon**.
😉

review_comments:
It has been too long since I last thought about the target tracking code in detail, and it took a concerted effort to get back into the mindset and remember the original reasoning behind this.

The idea behind this line was to separate the various cases into two bins: the target is an actor that is currently visible (→ `useLastVisibleTarget == false`) vs "we have no knowledge of the actor state this tick" (→ `useLastVisibleTarget == true`).

There are a bunch of different cases in this second bin*, but we define the same behavior for all of them: if we don't know the current location, move to the last known location. We will either recover vision in a future tick, or we'll reach the requested range of the last known target and the activity will end.

Note that this also covers the case where we saw the target die: we defined / decided as an intentional gameplay mechanic that units should continue moving within range of where the target died - in part because it makes the code so much simpler, but also because we felt it better for gameplay than units going idle at arbitrary times, potentially while in the middle of nowhere while moving long range.

This logic *should* work fine provided we can guarantee that `lastVisibleTarget` has a sensible value. If the activity ticks at least once with the target visible then we are fine. Otherwise, we rely on the information passed into the activity constructor. If we have neither there is no way to recover, and the `useLastVisibleTarget && !lastVisibleTarget.IsValidFor(self)` bails us out. #17227 would make this simpler and more correct.

*Off the top of my head, there may be more:
* Target is (alive or dead), but under the fog
* Target is (alive or dead), but represented by a frozen actor
* Target is dead, and we saw it die
* Target is alive, but conditions / transforming mean we can no target it (i had previously forgotten about this one)

With this context in place, can you outline the goal behaviour with the changes here?

Its not clear to me why the fix needs to change `useLastVisibleTarget`, and if the main motivation was to make units go idle when the target dies, then that is actually a significant change that we need to consider in more detail (and for more cases) - putting it outside the scope of this bugfix.

The context was pretty clear already, but thanks anyway.

We need to bail out of the activity as soon as the target is dead in order to address #16922. The change here makes the plane exit the activity when the target is known to have died (e.g. when the plane itself killed it), but move to the last known location if it's fate is unknown (and then then exit anyway if it cannot be found).

Yes, this also makes the plane exit the activity early when something else visibly killed it. This was not the motivation for the change here, but it seems a lot more sensible than the alternative anyway. There is no reason to go to that specific location and then idle anyway when the specific target of a focus fire order is already dead. If the player explicitly wanted the plane to go there regardless, they should have used an attack-move instead.

Yes, this should be changed for all the other activities that use this targetting logic as well for consistency, but that is not needed for the actual bugfix here.

> There is no reason to go to that specific location and then idle anyway when the specific target of a focus fire order is already dead.

The main reason is that this is the way all the other units have worked for the last couple of releases. Can we please introduce a `cancelOnTargetVisiblyRemoved` (ideally with a better variable name) flag to the `Fly` ctor so we can enable this behaviour when queued as a child of `FlyAttack`, but minimizes behaviour changes for anything else that queues it?

> it seems a lot more sensible than the alternative anyway.

This remains to be debated, ideally informed by examples from how other games handle it. I'm not convinced that units going idle at an arbitrary time/place (which may not be safe: e.g. infantry on Tiberium) and requiring the player to recover them is a better solution than completing the move to a location that we can assume probably has other enemy targets nearby.
I'd rather not get dragged into any 'debates' again.
Style nit: the bulk of our inline comments don't end with a full stop, so it looks odd here.

Currently it's a mess. There are many comments in the surrounding code which do have a full stop and many which don't—with no rhyme or reason. I always aim to use proper punctuation in my comments so I prefer to have it here as well.
Ok. I'm not going to force you to use incorrect punctuation :smile:

Removing this means that `AttackAircraftInfo.AttackTurnDelay` is no longer used. Is this intentional?

This will have implications for the agility/balancing of aircraft attack runs!

It was semi-intentional. Trying to still cram in `AttackTurnDelay` was a big mistake in #16945. The idea here is to always strafe until the maximum weapon range is reached, so that the next strafing pass will start at the optimal weapon range. Of course leaving in a parameter that is not used anywhere is not nice.

I think that thinking in terms of ranges and trajectories here is much nicer than an arbitrary tick count. If it turns out that we still need to tweak this knob, I think we should change `AttackTurnDelay` from a tick count to a `WDist` and have it replace `lastVisibleMaximumRange` in `MoveWithinRange` below when explicitly set.

If it saves us an update rule for now, we can do the same with the current `AttackTurnDelay` and use the speed of the aircraft to translate it into a comparable distance. I think it should be pointed out though that the latest changes to this parameter are likely based on false assumptions about the aircraft behaviour and should be taken with a grain of salt.
I really like the idea of specifying an attack run length instead of a tick delay. IMO the hassle of an update rule would be worth it here.
We'll need to remember to keep this when picking to prep.

In practice this check won't do much because the `CanHover` is typically inherited from a default template.
We support hovering units that strafe, so i don't think its valid to throw those out here anyway?

In that case, we can simplify down to:
```csharp
if (attackType != null && attackType.NodeValue<AirAttackType>() != AirAttackType.Strafe)
```

which fixes the false-positive reporting of the RA and TD helicopters.
We support hovering units that strafe, but we don't support non-hovering units that don't strafe, which is what is excluded here.
The issue here is that we are reporting units with `AirAttackType.Hover` in the `StrafeRunLength` notification, even though `StrafeRunLength` doesn't apply to them.

Yes, but otherwise we would theoretically skip units for which `StrafeRunLength` does apply. The issue is with FlyAttack.cs: L157. Even when the aircraft explicitly defines another `AttackType` it will still do a strafing run if it cannot hover. This is pretty counterintuitive though, so perhaps we should change that line and just allow the nonsensical behaviour. After all: `AttackType` defaults to `Strafe` anyway.

My main motivation is to remove the `Aircraft` node lookup because these kind of lookups don't reliably work from update rules. IMO its not worth the effort to notify the user that they can customize an already-broken configuration, which lead to my suggestion above.
I may be a bit confused here, but don't these lines mean that `lastVisibleTarget` could never be reassigned to an invalid target? So `lastVisibleTarget` would never be invalid in any case?
It can be invalid, see #17409 and #17415. Not sure how likely it is for aircraft to get shot from below fow/shroud and trying to retaliate (that is the example case for never seeing a target).
To clarify: Yes, it can't be assigned to invalid here, but it can be the case that it is never assigned at all.

> Not sure how likely it is for aircraft to get shot from below fow/shroud and trying to retaliate (that is the example case for never seeing a target).

It may be an issue to modders

Won't this fail if the turn radius is comparable or smaller than the minimum range?

One of the benefits / uses of `AttackAircraftInfo.AttackTurnDelay` was to allow modders/balancers to avoid this case.

If the plane is not past the center of the target annulus and the turn radius is much smaller than the minimum range, the plane will instantly turn around. If the turn radius is much larger it will keep moving forward with a slight bend until it reaches the target annulus at the other side. If the plane is past the center, it will just keep moving forward in a straight line. There is never a problem here.

I think you are a bit confused here: This has nothing to do with `AttackTurnDelay`; This is just generic `MoveWithinRange` behaviour.

The problem you are thinking of could theoretically occur, but only when the turn radius is _bigger_ than the _maximum_ weapon range. This case is already covered by the block ate lines 225–244 below.
